Title: Nothing new to say on Protect Thine Own

Messages.Author: The Lasombra
Messages.Body:
There are two sides to the argument about banning or changing Protect
Thine Own. This document will describe both sides of the argument,
but may not be complete. Every time you see banned, read it as
banned/changed.

Anti-banning / Anti-changing arguments:

1) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it was just
reprinted in the Camarilla Edition.
a) New players will be upset that they cannot play with it in
tournaments.
b) The current design team is god-like in their ability to
choose which cards to reprint. (See also: Twisting the Knife and Up
Yours!)

2) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it gives Inner
Circle members an action that justifies their high capacity and time
to influence into play.

3) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it gives Justicars
an action that justifies their high capacity and time to influence
into play.

4) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because other similar cards
exist, ie Sacrifice and Tradition Upheld.

5) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it is easily
countered with existing vote defense cards.

6) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it gives players the
opportunity to burn the key vampire from their opponent's deck because
their opponents chose to play with non-Camarilla vampires and does not
require risky combat or diablerie.

7) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it was designed by
Shawn F. Carnes, Paul Peterson, and Matt Burke and together they are
the holy trinity of trading card game design.

8) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because I need to be able to
eliminate my grand-prey's defensive vampire without any risk of being
blocked before he becomes my prey or I will not win the game.

9) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it can only effect
397 vampires in the game.

10) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it can only be
played by 20 vampires in the game, 7 Inner Circle members and 13
Justicars.

11) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because Direct Intervention
exists.

12) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it is not
dominating tournament play. Only 8 decks won tournaments out of the
last 115 when they had the card in their deck.

13) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because it is not causing
people to leave the tournament scene.

14) Protect Thine Own should not be banned because TheLasombra.com
still has 15 copies for sale and it must not be very good if it is
still in stock.

-----------------------------------
-----------------------------------

Pro-banning / Pro-changing arguments:

1) Protect Thine Own should be banned to protect new players that are
using Anarchs and Black Hand and do not have access to Delaying
Tactics or Direct Intervention as they were not printed in either set.

2) Protect Thine Own should be banned because it is too powerful of a
swing effect for 1 card, eliminating a vampire while it has no defense
(see Closed Session) or opportunity to block (when called cross-table)
is more than game ruining for the victim player.

3) Sacrifice should also not exist, and wisely has not been reprinted
since Sabbat. Tradition Upheld should not exist and has wisely not
been reprinted since Dark Sovereigns.

4) Protect Thine Own should be banned because it is not sufficiently
costed for the effect that it generates. Compare to Banishment, the
closest political action that non-Camarilla decks have access to, and
you find these additional abilities: PTO 1-move vampire to
uncontrolled (As Banishment), 2-remove all blood from uncontrolled
vampire to blood bank, 3-remove vampire from uncontrolled region to
ash heap.

5) If I can out-bloat or oust my prey faster than a vote deck can
reduce my pool to zero, that speed or bloat can be my vote defense. I
cannot use similar measures to defend against Protect Thine Own. I
must use Direct Intervention and Delaying Tactics in order to have a
chance to survive. Delaying Tactics will grant one turn reprieve, and
then I must have a second. If I must play with these cards
specifically to keep my vampires in the game (ie, I must play X or
anti-X), then the card should not be in the game. For all decks
designed around disciplines possessed only by independent clans or
Sabbat clans, I must play with these specific defenses. For all decks
designed around specific abilites granted by being Anarch or Black
Hand, I must play with these specific defenses. For all decks
designed around specific non-Camarilla vampires and their general
utility, I must play with these specific defenses. There are too many
decks that are too vulnerable to this card and that must play anti-X
to even be able to continue to play.

6) Protect Thine Own should be banned because it gives players the
opportunity to burn the key vampire from their opponents' deck because
their opponents chose to play with non-Camarilla vampires and does not
require risky combat or diablerie.

7) Protect Thine Own is from the same designers as Return to
Innocence, Tomb of Ramses, Mind Rape, and Thought's Betrayed, four of
the most broken cards in the game. This by itself is almost a good
enough reason to consider banning/changing the card.

8) Protect Thine Own should be banned because the ability to eliminate
your grand-prey's defensive vampire without any risk of being blocked
before he becomes your prey is too powerful.

9) Protect Thine Own should be banned because it can effect 397
vampires in the game, which is 57% of the vampires in the game.

10) Protect Thine Own should be banned because it can only be played
by 20 vampires in the game, 7 Inner Circle members and 13 Justicars,
and they are the most powerful and have access to the most powerful
cards already, see the Traditions as examples. All of these 20
vampires have access to Closed Session which completely removes the
victim's ability to interact in the referendum. Protect Thine Own
should be banned because there is no political action card that
provides the same level of fragility to the Camarilla vampires for the
non-Camarilla vampires to call.

11) Protect Thine Own should be banned because its only true defense
is Direct Intervention and playing Camarilla vampires exclusively in
tournaments.

12 - 13) Protect Thine Own should be banned because it constricts the
quantity of tournament caliber decks by its very existence. Strong
decks based on non-Camarilla vampires are not tournament options while
this card is allowed in the tournament setting. People playing to win
will choose anti-X (Camarilla decks) as long as X (Protect Thine Own)
continues to be allowed in tournaments. People are driven from the
tournament scene all the time, there is no reason to allow this to be
one more.

14) Protect Thine Own is bad for the game, rarity or availability of
the card has no bearing on this argument.

Many of these arguments assume that the action is unblockeable and the
referendum unassailable. Although the latter is often true, the
former, even crosstable, isn't. At least here in central Ohio it is
fairly common to see Eagle Sight (maybe not most tables, but I
wouldn't be surprised if at least one deck per table packed Eagle
Sight), and Draba helps a lot as well.
Actions *do* get blocked, and if people don't pack intercept (or
bounce, or combat defense) it's their funeral. Tough luck, and I
lament it myself at times, but good decks either run on their own
solo-strategy (e.g., Crypt Machine, weenie dementation bleed, etc) or
are able to manipulate the table somehow.

It could be the local playstyle, butI've always thought that there was
a serious opportunity cost to playing with PTO. You need an Inner
Circle member (for full effect), who cannot play the tradition and

My first answer is : no. This is a game with many different individuals, and
I think no one can come with a definition of anything that would be
universally accepted.

I can tell you what I put into the "ban or errate" category, though :

- the "You lose" cards. You intercept me ? Kiss of Râ, I burn 3, you go to
torpor and burn 2 (in effect, it's "go to torpor for one less blood than
what I paid"). I intercept you ? Aggrav, Rötschreck, you lose. No matter how
well you combat section is built, be it in pure fighting (anti-manoeuver,
anti-S:CE, big hits or aggravs, etc.) you just go to torpor, eventually get
amaranthed on the way, and SHUT UP ! Nice. What a pleasure playing in such
conditions, thank you, let's do it again tomorrow ? No thanks, I must go see
my dentist tomorrow. Less painful.
Although these cards don't give you the assurance of victory, they'll most
probably screw someone else's game. No card should have such an effect.

- the "play this" cards (what Derek walls "unfair") ; in that category, I of
course include PTO and J:CS. Better play Camarilla, or else you risk being
targetted by these ugly little things... I can't count the times I've seen a
game lost because Monçada, Thetmes, Carlotta, Le Din Tho or whoever was
burned by it (I once was lucky and wily enough to Delay one, and go with LDT
to see my prey's hand although he just had discarded it, and I often play
Possession ; should everybody include LDT or Necro to counter PTO ? Yes, of
course !!! ;)
Kiss of Râ could also be included in that category : play For, or else...

- Last but not least, the "universal" cards. They are included in most
tournament decks because they can do so many things, why not incude them ?
I'm not referring to Blood Dolls or Deflections, because 1) They are an
essential part of the basic mechanisms of the game, and 2) there are other
options for pool gain or against bleed, even if arguably less good ones.
These could include Sudden Reversals. And I would love to be able to play
bleed or vote without them but the decks would be much less effective. But
SR are a lesser evil : they target only master cards, which represent
roughly a 5th of each deck, sometimes less, and they take on you own master
cards space.
Direct Intervention can counter the other 4 fifths of everyone's decks. It
can counter a carefully established strategy, because nothing else in your
deck could counter this or that action, but Caine himself descends from on
high and... You lose ?! Yes, it can also fit that category. But in much
worse, because it reduces the variety of the game.
I also include Dreams of the Sphynx in the universal category, because it is
so good everyone includes them. I've even known some people to include 5 of
them in a bleed deck... ;-)

If I had a choice, the "play this" cards would be the ones I'd banish or
errate first : no part of the game should be discouraged. It isn't good for
game variety, and cannot be good commercially either (me, buy some indies ?
Why, to get burned ???)

The You lose cards would go next. And last but not least, the universal
ones.

So my Hate List is, in that order :

PTO, J:CS, DI, Rö, KoR, and eventually DotS (don't hate it that much, it's
just too good for what it costs).

Rather than argumenting for or against PTO specifically (as it
should be clear that I'm already in the camp that is unhappy
with the current wording of PTO) I'll try to verbalize an analyze
of some whys and whynots.

Most arguments have revolved around if a card is too strong or
not, but in reality we're adressing the circumstances around
an effect and the cost in opportunity or otherwise to achieve
that effect.

What is cost?

1) Blood
2) Pool
3) Requirements (clan, sect, capacity etc)
4) Number of cards needed (usually 1, but Choir for example requires
more)
5) Limitations (Only works on allies etc)
6) Type (I identify three types of effects where in ascending order
of cost they are Minion-cards, Master-cards and Vampires, and
perhaps Minion-cards would require a further split in subtypes)
7) Ease of use (usually varying degrees of inherent stealth or other
types of uncounterability, or, as we're talking cost, the lack
thereof)
8) Number of consequtive effects needed (Graverobbing requires the
torporizing of a vampire and so could be said to have a cost of
2 in this case)
9) Ease of countering (Discard a card to say NO, any minion can burn
this card as an action etc, etc)

What is the environment of an effect?

1) Time
1.1 Transient (Computer Hacking)
1.2 Lingering but restricted (KRCG News Radio)
1.3 Lingering (Mr. Winthrop)

2) Availability
2.1 Once per game (Giant's Blood)
2.2 Unique (Hunting Ground)
2.3 Max X per player/minion (Sportsbike)
2.4 Repeatable/Stackable (Flak Jacket)

3) Sideeffect
Examples are Trifle (Get extra MP), Untap after execution (Go Anarch)
and maybe more that I can't remember now.
Sideeffects I have defined as effects that are only there to offset
a Cost.

4) Impact
All the way from adding a blood to one of your vampires to 'Win the
Game'.

What is an effect?

Burn pool, intercept stealth, deal damage to another minion, burn a
card in play and so on and so on.

The feeling I have, this far, is that most people are confusing the
Impact of an effect with the effect itself, and that was the main
reason for my rather stupid stunt with arguing that Graverobbing
was a more broken card than PTO, because a succesful Graverobbing
does indeed have a greater Impact than a succcesful PTO.

Most players, and I'm included here, have this aversion to 'Move
controlled vampire to Ashheap', which is actually just an effect,
and one that has less Impact than 'Move controlled vampire to
opposing players Ready Region'.
However, the words 'Burn' combined with 'Vampire' have an emotional
value that is perhaps stronger than the underlying effect merits,
or rather merits when compared to other effects.

So, when checking if an effect is wellrounded we should compare
Cost with Environment.

Before you start yelling 'Doh, idiot, everyone does that without
your lecturing!' think for a while if that is really so.
I'm not certain that I always stay cool enough to do so, and I
know for certain that Cost and Environment are complex enough for
me to start resorting to comparing one card with another without
checking if that comparision is really valid.

Now, back to PTO.

Cost:

1) 1 blood
2) 0 pool
3) Inner Circle or (for a sidecost) Justicar
4) 1 card
5) Non-camarilla (Justicar sidecost being max-capacity of target)
6) Minion-card
7) +1 stealth and 1 vote (In other words a negative cost)
8) 1 effect needed
9) Undirected, so two blockers rather than one. A few cards in the
game can counter PTO directly. Can be stopped during referendum
by voting it down

Environment:

1) Transient
2) Repeatable/Stackable
3) None
4) High-medium I'd say. A High Impact would be Oust prey

Effect:

Move one vampire from controlled region to ash-heap.

Reading the costs I can only see two worth mentioning, being
of course the rather hefty requirements and the actually rather
severe limitation on what can be targeted.

The Environment is very friendly for this effect.

The effect is one which can be reached by other means than using
PTO, so a comparision is valid.

Diablerie and other cards burning vampires in torpor. We can agree
that the Environment is identical, but what about Cost? (Actually
Sacrificial Lamb has a more beneficial environment in terms of
Impact)

Diablerie doesn't have a blood cost, Vulnerability costs a pool
and Sacrificial Lamb costs three blood. Decapitate costs 2 blood.
On average higher cost if there is a cost at all.

Diablerie can be commited by just about anyone, so lower cost.
Sacrificial Lamb and Decapitate requires a discipline at superior
which is a lower cost compared to PTO.
Vulnerability is a Master-type effect, which is a higher cost.

All require target in torpor or on its way there. Diablerie has
a zero card-cost, but you risk your acting vampire in the following
Bloodhunt. However, we can burn anything in torpor.
Severe limitation on target availability is a higher cost.
Lower limitation on type of target is a lower cost.

All are directed at the target, so only one blocker rather than two.
Now it can be debated if this is a lower cost or not, but usually
undirected actions are considered more expensive than directed ones
when it comes to ease of blocking, so I'll stick to it being so in
this case as well.
Directed action is a lower cost.

All are at zero stealth (Ok, Nos player could stealth its way to the
combat where it's going to play Decapitate).
Lack of inherent stealth is a higher cost.
Vulnerability is either Suddened Reversaled or succcesful, so has
a lower cost.

Sending a vampire to torpor is an effect in itself.
Higher cost in terms of number of effects required.

In terms of ease of countering the lowest cost goes to Vulnerability,
Sacrificial Lamb and Decapitate, and the highest cost here
is actually held by PTO as it's not sufficient to make a succesful
action.

This is no answer to if PTO is undercosted or not, just a statement
that there are more ways in the game to achieve the same effect
that PTO does, that there does indeed exist a method for comparision
between those ways.
More importantly it's an attempt to put the light on the diffference
between an effect and the environment of an effect.

Sten During

I'm sure the number of vampires capable of playing the card, while it
is not to be neglected, is far less significant for single discipline
cards than it would seem.

Because on the one hand you will not be able to include the card in a
deck where few vampires can play it, but on the other, you can compose
a deck whose crypt is selected partly for the ability to play the
given card.

Sometimes a single card can make a strong asset in a deck (perhaps
with multiple copies). Example would be the (for example) Tremere deck
which uses small and large vampires and has lots of Govern (in which
case the fatties recruit the weenies for you).

Costing: Sometimes an effect will cost more for certain disciplines.
I'm viewing this like this: For every discipline, there is a set of
exceptional effects, like Stealth for Obfuscate. There may also be a
set of favored effects (Stealth for Obtenebration), available effects
(Stealth from Dementation), hindered effects (Stealth from Celerity),
and non-existent effects (Stealth from any non-stealthy discipline).

However, from the point of view of the individual cards there are
usually only three levels (for general effects):

1 <of something> for free at inferior
1 <of something> for 1 blood at inferior or for free at superior
1 <of something> for 2 blood at inferior or for 1 blood at superior

Also, an action could probably be measured in the amount of blood/pool
manipulation. Restoration-type effects show a good head start:

action with no discipline and no card - 1 blood
action with inferior discipline and 1 card played - 2 blood
action with superior discipline and 1 card played - 3 blood

How about assigning the following values:

action - worth 1 blood
action + card (+ inferior) - worth 2 blood
action + card + superior - worth 3 blood

If the cost increases, so does the effect. Extreme effects will likely
increase the cost beyond the linear.
Example card: Heavy Bleed. Presence, 1 blood, (D) bleed at +2 Bleed /
<sup> +3 bleed.
Another: Extreme Bleed. Presence, 3 blood, (D) bleed at +3 bleed /
<sup> +4 bleed.

Just some ideas... ;)

I'd add Vox Domini and Delaying Tactics here. DI burns the current
